title: Law & Your Rights · Episode 2
chapters: Separation of powers: why no one holds all the keys
Marbury v Madison: how courts got the power to strike down laws
Contracts: the deals you make every day

units.t: Law & Your Rights. Episode two.

In this episode: The Australian Constitution, Separation of powers: why no one holds all the keys, Marbury v Madison: how courts got the power to strike down laws and Contracts: the deals you make every day.
Part one. The Australian Constitution.
A document written by colonial delegates in the 1890s still decides who can make which laws, and only the voters can change it.
Six colonies, one nation.
Before 1901, Australia was six British colonies with their own parliaments, tariffs and even railway gauges.
Through the 1890s, delegates met at conventions to draft a federal constitution.
Unusually for the time, voters approved it at colonial referendums, and the British Parliament passed it as the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900.
The Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901.
The Constitution is short, around 128 sections, and freely available online.
Federation meant dividing power.
Section 51 lists about 40 subjects for Commonwealth laws, including defence, taxation, trade between states, marriage, immigration, currency and postal services.
Everything unlisted stays with the states, which run police, schools, hospitals and most criminal law.
If a valid Commonwealth law conflicts with a state law, section 109 makes the state law invalid to the extent of the inconsistency.
How it's built.
The Constitution is organised into chapters.
Chapter I creates the Parliament: the King, represented by the Governor-General, the Senate and the House of Representatives.
Chapter II covers the executive government, which puts laws into action.
Chapter III establishes the High Court and other federal courts.
Australia is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy.
The Senate gives each original state the same number of senators regardless of population, 12 each since 1984, protecting smaller states.
The House of Representatives is based on population, and the party or coalition that controls it forms government.
Power drifts to Canberra.
The founders expected the states to stay powerful, but the balance has shifted.
In the Engineers' Case of 1920, the High Court began reading Commonwealth powers broadly.
During World War II, the Commonwealth took over income tax, the High Court upheld the scheme, and that is why income tax is now collected federally.
Section 96 lets the Commonwealth give states money on conditions, so it can shape areas like schools and hospitals that it doesn't directly control.
The gap between who raises the money and who spends it is called vertical fiscal imbalance, and it drives constant federal and state negotiation.
Separate powers.
The Constitution separates three arms of government: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets and applies them.
In Australia, the legislature and executive are closely linked, because ministers must sit in parliament and answer to it.
This is called responsible government.
The separation of judicial power is much stricter.
In the Boilermakers' Case, 1956, the High Court held that federal courts can exercise only judicial power, and bodies that aren't courts can't exercise it.
This protects judges' independence, so courts can rule against the government of the day without fear.
Changing it, and your rights.
Under section 128, the Constitution changes only by referendum.
A change needs a double majority: a majority of voters nationally and a majority in at least four of the six states.
Only eight of 45 proposals since 1901 have succeeded.
In 1967, over 90 per cent voted to let the Commonwealth make laws for Aboriginal people and count them in the population; the 1999 republic and 2023 Voice proposals failed.
There is no national bill of rights.
The Constitution has few express rights, such as jury trial for serious Commonwealth offences and 'just terms' for acquired property.
In 1992 the High Court found an implied freedom of political communication, not a general free speech right.
Most protections come from ordinary laws, which parliament can change.
Read the official Yes and No cases before voting.
This is general information only.
The key idea: The Constitution united six colonies in 1901 and divides law-making power between the Commonwealth and the states.
Part two. Separation of powers: why no one holds all the keys.
Who makes the laws, who carries them out, and who decides what they mean?
Keeping those three jobs apart is one of the oldest safeguards against tyranny, and Australia does it in its own distinctive way.
Three keys to one vault.
Imagine a vault that needs three keys turned at once, held by three different people.
No one can empty it alone.
That is the idea behind the separation of powers.
The legislature makes laws; in Australia, that is Parliament.
The executive runs the country day to day, including the Prime Minister, ministers and the public service.
The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes: the courts.
If one group controlled all three, it could write any rule, enforce it however it liked and judge its own case.
The French thinker Montesquieu made the case in The Spirit of the Laws, 1748: liberty is at risk when one body both makes and enforces laws, or when judges are not separate from rulers.
His reading of England was imperfect, but his argument shaped modern democracies.
The American model.
The framers of the United States Constitution in 1787 took Montesquieu seriously.

They placed Congress, the President and the Supreme Court in separate articles and kept their members apart: the President does not sit in Congress, and members of Congress cannot serve in the cabinet.
They added checks and balances so each branch can restrain the others.
The President can veto bills, Congress can override a veto with a large enough majority, the Senate must approve many appointments, and the courts can strike down laws that breach the Constitution.
Supporters say this makes power hard to abuse.
Critics say it can make government slow and prone to deadlock when rival parties control different branches.
Australia's blend.
Australia's founders borrowed from two traditions.
From the United States came a written Constitution with separate chapters: Chapter I covers Parliament, Chapter II the executive and Chapter III the courts.
From Britain came the Westminster system of responsible government, where ministers must sit in Parliament and answer to it.
Section 64 says a minister must become a senator or member of the House within three months.
So Parliament and the executive overlap heavily: the government is formed by whoever holds the confidence of the House of Representatives.
What keeps this in check is that ministers can be questioned in Parliament every sitting day, can lose the House's confidence, and must face voters at regular elections.
Keeping judges apart.
Where Australia is strict is the judiciary.

In the landmark 1956 Boilermakers' Case, the High Court ruled that a federal body could not combine judicial power, such as deciding legal guilt and punishment, with non-judicial functions like setting wages through arbitration.
Judicial power under Chapter III must be exercised by courts, and courts should not be handed tasks that compromise their independence.
Later cases extended some protection to state courts too, because they can exercise federal power.
Judges are also protected in other ways.
Federal judges can be removed only by the Governor-General after both houses of Parliament ask, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, and their pay cannot be cut while they hold office.
Checks in everyday politics.
Once you know what to look for, checks appear everywhere.
The Senate rejecting or amending a bill is one house checking another.
Senate estimates hearings, where officials are grilled on spending, are Parliament checking the executive.
A court ruling a government decision unlawful is the judiciary checking the executive.
Auditors-General, ombudsmen and anti-corruption commissions add more, and a free press and the right to vote act as checks from outside government.
There is no perfect division.
Separate power too strictly and government can grind to a halt.
Concentrate it and those in charge may escape accountability.
Britain relies heavily on convention, the United States has rigid separation, and Australia sits between.
People tend to value checks more when their side is out of power.
The key idea: Government power splits into three jobs, and keeping them apart makes abuse of power harder.
Part three. Marbury v Madison: how courts got the power to strike down laws.
A row over an undelivered job letter gave judges one of the greatest powers in modern government.
The judge who did it managed to win by appearing to lose.
The midnight commission.
John Adams and the Federalists lost the 1800 election to Thomas Jefferson.
Before handing over in March 1801, Adams created new judicial posts and filled them with Federalists, whom critics called the midnight judges.
One was William Marbury, named a justice of the peace for the District of Columbia.
His commission was signed and sealed, but in the last-minute rush the Secretary of State's office failed to deliver it.
That Secretary of State was John Marshall, who had just become Chief Justice.
When Jefferson took office, his Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to hand it over.
Marbury sued directly in the Supreme Court, seeking a writ of mandamus, an order commanding an official to do his legal duty.
Winning by losing.
The case was a trap.
If Marshall ordered Madison to deliver the commission, the administration would probably ignore him, exposing the young Court as powerless.
If he backed down, he would seem to concede that the executive could ignore the law.
In February 1803, Marshall ruled that Marbury had a right to his commission and the law should provide a remedy.
But the Supreme Court could not provide it.
The section of the Judiciary Act that let Marbury come directly to the Court tried to expand its original jurisdiction beyond what the Constitution allowed.
When an ordinary law conflicts with the Constitution, the Constitution must win.
So Marbury lost, and Jefferson got his result.
But the Court had claimed something far bigger: the power to declare acts of Congress unconstitutional.
Judges say the law.
Marshall's reasoning was straightforward.
A written constitution is the supreme law, deliberately placed above ordinary laws.
If Congress could pass any law regardless of the Constitution, its limits would be meaningless.
Someone must decide whether a law conflicts with it, and Marshall argued that this job belonged to judges.
In one of the most quoted lines in American law, he wrote that it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.
This is judicial review.
The Constitution had not spelled it out clearly, though some founders had discussed the idea.
Marshall made it settled doctrine, using a case where his ruling gave his political opponents a short-term win.
A sleeping giant.
For such an important power, judicial review was used sparingly at first.
After Marbury, the Supreme Court did not strike down another act of Congress until 1857, in the infamous Dred Scott decision.
It held that Black Americans could not be citizens and helped push the country towards civil war.
Judicial review is a tool, and courts can use it badly as well as wisely.
Over time the power grew.
In the 20th century, the Court struck down laws on everything from segregated schools to campaign spending.
Because judges are unelected, debates continue about how boldly they should use this power, and when they should defer to elected lawmakers.
Those debates are as old as the decision itself.
Down under and beyond.
The idea spread to many countries with written constitutions.
Australia's framers built a federal system in which the Commonwealth's powers are limited, so it was taken for granted that the High Court would decide whether laws stayed within those limits.
In the 1951 Communist Party case, Justice Fullagar wrote that in our system the principle of Marbury v Madison is accepted as axiomatic, meaning self-evident.
The United Kingdom is different.
Under parliamentary sovereignty, British courts cannot strike down an Act of Parliament.
Since the Human Rights Act 1998 they can declare a law incompatible with protected rights, but Parliament decides whether to change it.
Different systems, different answers to the question of who has the final word.
The key idea: An undelivered job letter from the outgoing president took William Marbury straight to the Supreme Court.
Part four. Contracts: the deals you make every day.
Your morning coffee, your phone plan and your job are all contracts.
Knowing how they work helps you avoid nasty surprises.
Agreements the law enforces.
A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce.
You make them constantly: buying a coffee, tapping onto public transport, signing up for a streaming service, accepting a job or leasing a flat.
In Australia, contract law comes mainly from judge-made common law, with legislation like the Australian Consumer Law layered on top to protect consumers.
Every contract starts with an offer: a clear promise to be bound on certain terms.

Goods on a shelf and most advertisements are usually only an 'invitation to treat', which is why a shop usually isn't obliged to sell a wrongly priced item, although misleading pricing can breach consumer law.
Acceptance must match the offer.
'I'll take it for $50 less' is a counter-offer, which rejects the original.
What makes it binding.
Courts generally look for offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, capacity and reasonably certain terms.
Consideration means each side gives or promises something: you pay, the café hands over coffee.
So a bare promise of a gift usually can't be enforced.
It needn't be fair: selling a car for one dollar can be valid, though a court may check for pressure or deception.
A deed can bind without consideration.
Business deals are presumed to be legally binding; family and social arrangements, like cooking dinner for a friend, are presumed not to be.
Under-18s can often escape contracts, with exceptions such as necessities, and rules vary by state.
Someone lacking mental capacity may also be able to avoid a contract.
Written or verbal.
A common myth is that a contract must be written and signed.
Most can be verbal, or formed through emails, texts or clicking 'I agree' online.
The problem with verbal contracts is proof: in a dispute, it's your word against theirs.
Some contracts must be in writing to be enforceable, notably contracts for the sale of land and certain consumer credit contracts.
For anything important, like building work, a loan to a friend or a business arrangement, put the key terms in writing.
Include the price, what's being delivered, deadlines and what happens if things go wrong.
When a deal is broken.
Failing to do what a contract requires is a breach.
The usual remedy is damages: money to put you in the position you'd have been in had the contract been performed, not to punish the other side.
For a serious breach, such as breaking an essential term, the innocent party may be able to end the contract.
Occasionally a court orders actual performance, called specific performance, mostly for unique things like land.
Contracts can also be set aside for misrepresentation, duress or unconscionable conduct.
Time limits apply to claims, commonly six years in many states.
Unfair terms and cooling-off.

In take-it-or-leave-it contracts, like phone plans, the Australian Consumer Law protects against unfair terms: those causing a significant imbalance that aren't reasonably necessary to protect the business, such as letting only one side change the price.
A court can void it, and since November 2023 relying on unfair terms is also illegal.
Many people believe every contract has a cooling-off period.
It doesn't: those rights exist only where a law or the contract creates them.
Unsolicited sales, such as door-to-door, carry 10 business days under the Australian Consumer Law.
Residential property buyers usually get a few days, such as five business days in NSW, but not at auction.
Never sign under pressure.
This is general information only; for big contracts, see a lawyer or Legal Aid.
The key idea: A contract is an agreement the law will enforce, and it needs a clear offer matched by acceptance.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What happens to a state law that conflicts with a valid Commonwealth law?
Answer. The state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency.
Question two. Why does splitting government into three branches protect against abuse?
Answer. No one group can make, enforce and judge the rules.
Question three. Why was Marshall in a political trap?
Answer. Ordering it risked defiance; refusing risked looking weak.
Question four. Why isn't a shop usually obliged to sell an item that was wrongly priced?
Answer. Shelf prices are usually just an invitation to treat.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
